look_here_first: LITTLE BLUESTEM (native): follow ONE entire flowering stem: many leafy upper branches each end in a separate short silky raceme, typically one short raceme per branch. KR bluestem (introduced) makes a compact cluster of longer fingerlike racemes at one terminal region. For plants with no seedheads, examine the truly KEELED/flattened leaf sheaths and the collar on an intact low tussock: do not confuse sheath-edge hairs with the true 0.5–2.5 mm membranous, often fringed LIGULE, or treat red color as identification proof. A physically archived spikelet-pair close-up is present; its reduced stalked partner varies across little-bluestem varieties. The new USGS sheath photo is a labelled, provisional first step toward a measured collar macro.
project_tracker_diagnostic: Diagnostic sequence for Central Texas: (1) numerous lateral leafy branches, each with its own 1–3 inch short raceme; (2) tight distinct base; (3) flattened/keeled sheaths and more obvious small ligule; (4) generally non-papillose blade surface above collar; (5) paired spikelets and hairy raceme axis at seed. Compared to invasive KR's several 3–8 (sometimes more) long clustered terminal fingers and often papilla-based upper-blade hairs. Fall color is NOT proof.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Voucher-based Texas Hill Country flora documents the species in multiple target-zone counties, including Hays; BONAP independently supports Texas native distribution.

morphology_keys.habit: Perennial warm-season grass forming distinct, relatively tight bunches.
morphology_keys.culms: Upper culms branch; each branchlet commonly terminates in a short raceme.
morphology_keys.leaves: Narrow blades; basal foliage and stems can develop reddish, copper, or mahogany tones late in the season.
morphology_keys.sheath_and_ligule: Upper and basal leaf sheaths are often conspicuously compressed/keeled with a longitudinal ridge; the sheath may be hairy even where nodes and blades are not. A membranous ligule is present and comparatively prominent in local Hays material. Photograph leaf blade, membranous collar and the keel as one continuous specimen; the precise ligule and hair pattern are not yet photo-arrow verified on this card. Reference bounds differ: FNA 0.5–2 mm; POWO/GrassBase 1–3 mm with eciliate membrane description; SDSU calls the ligule fringed (<2.5 mm). These reflect source/taxon variation or character interpretations. Do not assert that every little-bluestem ligule has an equally visible fringe; isolate the TRUE membrane vs nearby sheath hairs with a millimeter ruler.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Numerous upper lateral leafy branches each end in a SINGLE short raceme (often about 2.5–7.5 cm, length variable); the short plume arises individually from a small upper sheath. KR's longer narrow racemes attach together in a terminal panicle, usually clustered 3–8 in Texas A&M's treatment, but Williamson County local flora reports up to 17 in complex plants.
morphology_keys.spikelets: Paired spikelets occur along the raceme; the fertile sessile spikelet bears a twisted/bent awn. The sessile fertile member contains TWO florets (upper fertile, lower sterile) within g1/g2 glumes, with upper lemma bearing bent/twisted awn. The companion PEDICELLATE member can be sterile reduced or more developed/staminate; Harms's A/F/P labels refer to axis, fertile sessile, pedicelled mate, NOT three fertile spikelets. Author dissection labels g1/g2/l_f/l_s/p_s on separately arranged parts.
best_field_traits: TOP PRIORITY — on a flowering shoot, find MANY leafy upper side branches and a short individual raceme (spikelet-bearing finger) at the end of EACH; trace where they originate rather than judging hairiness.
Against KR: look for several LONG narrow racemes gathered at one terminal panicle in KR; little bluestem usually bears separate SHORT silky racemes inserted at multiple upper leaves.

NO SEEDHEAD — little bluestem usually forms a tight persistent bunch with distinctly flattened/keeled basal leaf sheaths; its true ligule is relatively conspicuous in local comparisons. Habit alone cannot exclude mown KR.

LEAF COLLAR — blades/nodes generally without KR's stiff, long papilla-based upper-blade hairs immediately above the ligule; verify from 2–3 intact leaves with magnification. KR node hairiness varies and is not a trustworthy binary test.

SEED STAGE — an individual short raceme has white silky hairs on rachis joints/pedicels, paired sessile fertile and reduced pedicelled spikelets, and a bent/twisted awn; a 1-mm ruler is needed for anatomical confirmation.
Red, copper, blue-green, orange, or silver fall appearance is supporting only, never decisive for a removal/seed collection decision.

advanced_confirmation.Trace the base of each flowering raceme: Little: from different leafy upper branch tips, each with its own tiny sheath. KR: multiple long racemes emerging near one terminal panicle axis.
advanced_confirmation.Nonflowering specimen: Flattened keeled leaf sheath, tight basal clump, relatively smooth upper blade near collar, small ligule and comparison with actual KR leaf blade; mowed KR may mimic bunching.
advanced_confirmation.Under 10–20×: Little: white-hairy rachis/pedicels and paired spikelet positions on a short branch; KR also has paired spikelets, so NOT by pairing alone. Verify whole attached flowering architecture.
advanced_confirmation.Seasonal caution: Before seed maturity racemes have appressed spikelets and few visible bent awns, so wait for mature head when architecture remains uncertain.
advanced_confirmation.Management safety: Do not authorize herbicide, mechanical removal, mowing as an invasive or native seed collection solely from color, tuft shape or an isolated detached fuzzy head.

what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Hays County whole, rooted, flowering plant showing persistent bunch and entire upper branching architecture.
Close view showing one short raceme inserted into each upper sheath, and several others on the same culm, with millimeter reference.
Same-plant keeled leaf sheath and true membranous/ciliate ligule photographed at 10–20×.
Dissected rachis and mature spikelet pair—fertile sessile spikelet, reduced pedicelled partner, lemma awn and hairs—against 1 mm ruler.
Side-by-side KR bluestem, cane bluestem, and silver bluestem, using independently identified Hays specimens with similar magnification.

comparisons.key_distinctions: At flowering, first trace RACEME ORIGINS: LITTLE has numerous short solitary racemes on separate leafy upper branches; KR has multiple long narrow racemes in one terminal head. At nonflowering stage LITTLE has a notably flattened/keeled sheath and often a well-defined persistent basal bunch; KR can spread from a flatter crown and develop stiff papilla-based blade hairs above its collar. KR can have hairy or smooth nodes depending on local material; node hairlessness is NOT proof. Matched mature spikelets and same-plant collars close the uncertain cases.

detailed_pair.title: Native little bluestem versus introduced KR bluestem — Central Texas crew key
detailed_pair.memory_rule: KR = a handful of LONG fingerlike racemes in one terminal cluster; LITTLE = SHORT racemes repeated on branches throughout the upper culm.
quick_split: KR bluestem (*Bothriochloa ischaemum*, often locally called var. songarica): the terminal seedhead is a cluster of several relatively long, narrow spicate racemes, often 3–8; these may appear fingerlike or subdigitate. The central axis is commonly shorter than its racemes. Light green or straw culms often spread and kink at nodes. Stiff papilla-based hairs on the upper leaf surface just above the collar support identification.

Little bluestem (*Schizachyrium scoparium*): a more distinct narrow perennial bunch. The upper culm divides into multiple leafy branches, with separate SHORT racemes at branch tips and from upper leaf sheaths, rather than all flowering branches gathering at one terminal center. Each raceme becomes silky/fluffy with mature seed; bluish green growing-season stems can redden, but color alone never proves species.
detailed_pair.important_correction: CAUTION: do not tell crew that all KR bluestem nodes must be hairless. Texas A&M describes smooth nodes in its songarica treatment, while UT Austin local work (Bob Harms and Williamson County flora) describes short or appressed hairs. Node pubescence can vary among local/hybrid concepts and is not a safe single-character distinction. B. barbinodis, cane bluestem, has conspicuously BEARDED nodes; compare its heavier hair tufts separately.
not_diagnostic_alone: flat or rounded bunch shape after mowing
one node with or without short hairs
photographer's original species label without actual botanical character confirmation
field_sequence: 1. Stand back and photograph an ENTIRE rooted plant: KR may be sprawling and crowding neighbors; little bluestem generally forms a tighter persistent bunch.

2. Follow each flowering branch to its ORIGIN. KR: 3–8 or more relatively long racemes cluster near one terminal panicle center. Little: many short racemes distributed on different upper side branches.
3. Part an intact leaf sheath at the collar. Look for a small ligule and, on suspected KR, the stiff long papilla-based hairs on blade ABOVE the collar. Photograph at 10× with a mm reference.

4. Inspect 2–3 mature flowering units under a lens: their paired sessile fertile / pedicelled companion spikelets, bristles and bent/twisted awns. In little bluestem, check the short raceme's hairy axis segments and pedicel remnants.
5. If seedheads are absent or flowering-stage transitional, mark 'bluestem sp., KR suspected' rather than treating native *Schizachyrium* as an invasive.

lookalikes.cue: Native cane bluestem; conspicuous long beard of hairs at stem nodes and often a broader fanlike panicle. The BEARD is heavier than ordinary short hairs occasionally noted on KR.
Native silver bluestem; a dense cottony silvery head with many short fuzzy branches rather than KR's few longer slender fingers.

Introduced Kleberg bluestem; can have several fingerlike awned racemes and white-ringed nodes. Check leaf collar, node and mature spikelet morphology; do not classify every KR-looking grass from panicle alone.
Native bushy bluestem; a bulky brushy plume composed of crowded silky racemes, commonly in moist sites, unlike distributed short little-bluestem racemes.
Native little bluestem; distributed SHORT axillary/terminal racemes among numerous upper branches rather than a tight terminal cluster of LONG fingers.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Follow one complete upper culm from the flag leaf to EVERY flowering branch. Inspect the upper blade surface immediately above its ligule.
field_matrix.little_bluestem: Separate SHORT silky racemes end many leafy lateral branches, usually one unit per sheath. The sheath may be sharply keeled; the blade usually lacks long stiff papillose hairs near its collar.
field_matrix.look_alike: KR makes several much LONGER narrow fingers in a terminal cluster, generally 3–8 in Texas A&M; up to 17 in complex regional flora. KR often has scattered long stiff papilla-based hairs immediately above collar.
field_matrix.no_seedhead: A tight perennial base + keeled sheath favors little, spreading/kinked stems + papilla-based collar hairs favors KR; take more than one leaf and do not treat habit as a final answer.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Several long fingers all connected near ONE central panicle = KR candidate; numerous separate short racemes on leafy side branches = native LITTLE candidate. Under uncertainty preserve the plant.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Count the relatively stout exposed flowering fingers and inspect their common attachment point.
field_matrix.little_bluestem: Many short individual racemes at distinct upper leafy branch tips.
field_matrix.look_alike: Big has a few comparatively stout exposed turkey-foot-like racemes clustered together (commonly 2–6); inspect complete tip and spikelets.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Few stout fingers at one tip = BIG; numerous separate short fluffy plumes along upper shoots = LITTLE.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Inspect entire silhouette; part the cottony head to see hidden short paired racemes and their spathe-like bracts.
field_matrix.little_bluestem: Multiple individual short racemes arise from spaced leafy upper branches rather than one compact brush.
field_matrix.look_alike: Bushy has a densely crowded, often broad oblong cottony crown with many short paired rames packed together, commonly at moist sites.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Big broad dense brush = BUSHY candidate; distinct separated short upper branch tips = LITTLE candidate.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Inspect how paired rames sit inside and emerge from long, flattened spathe-like sheaths.
field_matrix.little_bluestem: Generally single short raceme per upper leafy branch/sheath; distinguish in several units.
field_matrix.look_alike: Broomsedge usually holds paired hairy rames partly within more conspicuous longer flattened spathes; narrow upper flowering outline.
field_matrix.quick_rule: One short raceme per upper leafy branch favors LITTLE; paired sheath-held flowering units favor BROOMSEDGE.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Inspect two true culm nodes just above the leaf sheath and the complete silver inflorescence.
field_matrix.little_bluestem: Short individual branch-end racemes; tight bunch without a distinctive ring of long silky hairs around every true node.
field_matrix.look_alike: Cane has a conspicuous long soft white beard at stem nodes and broad multi-branched fanlike seedhead.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Heavy true node beard + broad fan = CANE; separate short silky upper branchlets = LITTLE.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Trace whether flowering units make a narrow contracted cottony head or independent upper leafy branches.
field_matrix.little_bluestem: Upper leafy branches each carry an individual short silky raceme, not a singular narrow cotton column.
field_matrix.look_alike: Silver is a compact narrow white-silky plume with numerous SHORT crowded branches and usually smooth pale nodes.
field_matrix.quick_rule: One narrow cottony panicle with many crowded short rames = SILVER candidate; distributed separate racemes = LITTLE.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Check mature terminal raceme-group arrangement, true nodes, ligule and complete reproductive structure.
field_matrix.little_bluestem: Different leafy upper branch origins with individual shorter racemes and characteristic keeled sheaths.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced Kleberg can mimic the terminal fingerlike KR bluestem silhouette; swollen or whitish node/raceme details require regional key.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Do not call every fingered nonnative-looking grass KR or confuse it with native little without attached full head and collar.

not_reliable_alone: Red, orange, bluish or tan leaf and stem color — weather, genetics and season cause overlap.
Fluffy white awned spikelets: several bluestems have them; trace WHERE flowering branches originate.
Size/height or tightly bunched appearance alone; mowing and drought alter both.
One smooth stem node on KR: some Hays-area variants have short appressed hairs; never enforce glabrous KR nodes.
A detached tuft of seedhead material that does not show its original attachment.
Source-labelled photo alone when it lacks the necessary anatomy.

ecological_notes.habitat: Prairies, savannas, open limestone sites, roadsides, and restoration areas across the Edwards Plateau and Blackland Prairie.

crew_field_sequence: 1. Stand back and photograph an ENTIRE rooted plant: KR may be sprawling and crowding neighbors; little bluestem generally forms a tighter persistent bunch.

2. Follow each flowering branch to its ORIGIN. KR: 3–8 or more relatively long racemes cluster near one terminal panicle center. Little: many short racemes distributed on different upper side branches.
3. Part an intact leaf sheath at the collar. Look for a small ligule and, on suspected KR, the stiff long papilla-based hairs on blade ABOVE the collar. Photograph at 10× with a mm reference.

4. Inspect 2–3 mature flowering units under a lens: their paired sessile fertile / pedicelled companion spikelets, bristles and bent/twisted awns. In little bluestem, check the short raceme's hairy axis segments and pedicel remnants.
5. If seedheads are absent or flowering-stage transitional, mark 'bluestem sp., KR suspected' rather than treating native *Schizachyrium* as an invasive.

field_id_finish_pass.science_guardrails: CAUTION: do not tell crew that all KR bluestem nodes must be hairless. Texas A&M describes smooth nodes in its songarica treatment, while UT Austin local work (Bob Harms and Williamson County flora) describes short or appressed hairs. Node pubescence can vary among local/hybrid concepts and is not a safe single-character distinction. B. barbinodis, cane bluestem, has conspicuously BEARDED nodes; compare its heavier hair tufts separately.

classification_checks.accepted: Schizachyrium scoparium (Michx.) Nash accepted by Kew POWO
classification_checks.upper_stem_character: Separate short racemes at ends of upper leafy branches, lower shoots tightly tufted, compare KR with longer terminal clustered fingers; branching architecture is stronger than color/one-hair character
classification_checks.spikelet_pair: Sessile spikelet has two florets, usually upper fertile bisexual and lower sterile; its paired pedicelled partner is often reduced sterile, but can vary and be staminate/awned. Do not teach fixed tiny pedicellate rudiment throughout species.
classification_checks.ligule_length: Flora of North America 0.5–2 mm; Kew/GrassBase 1–3 mm; USDA instructional source approximately 0.5–2.5 mm. Photographic threshold: measure actual opened membrane using real mm scale; do not demand an exact constant length or that hair fringe must always be conspicuous.
classification_checks.ligule_fringe_variation: GrassBase explicitly describes eciliate membrane; SDSU educational account describes fringed membrane. Treat marginal ciliation/hairs as variable descriptions and record what the actual source-vouched plant shows; differentiate long sheath-margin hairs from ligule membrane.
classification_checks.native_and_county: Kew accepts native Canada–Mexico; independent UT DigFlora documents North Hays, no new native-range field changes here.
classification_checks.photo_pixel_truth: Author's A/F/P and glume/lemma labels externally verified as such; other original 15 broad in-gallery arrows remain provisional user review, not a substitute for exact in-situ reconstructed mm-scale anatomical arrows.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Little bluestem — verified Hays labelled ligule, A/F/P pair, detached spikelet, roots and KR comparison
steps: 1. See the existing real green bunch and Bob Harms photo 8 (SCSC-a) for a truly densely tufted plant with closely grouped basal culms. Photo 9 is a mixed prairie context; do not identify background grasses by color.
2. Trace photo 10 (SCSC-i): multiple short independent racemes arise from different leafy UPPER branches, unlike several clustered long terminal fingers on KR B. ischaemum.

3. Compare early flowering photo 2 (Judy Gallagher anthers) with Bob Harms photos 11–12 (SCSC-J/J1). Brown-purple dangling structures are anthers; airy white hairs on ripe rachis are separate dispersal adaptations, NOT aster-style pappus.

4. Photo 13 (SCSC-s) shows an ACTUAL attached mature awned raceme with hairy rachis/pedicel area. Find one awned sessile fertile unit and smaller pedicelled companion at a node; its exact mm length is NOT measured from this unscaled view.

5. Photo 14 (SCSC-9) shows physically detached original little-bluestem spikelet/bract parts with an actual ruler. DO NOT join neighboring detached pieces conceptually into one falsely identified attached spikelet pair.
6. Photo 15 (SCSC-C) proves visible flattened culm, a node, green overlapping sheath and long sheath hairs; those are not the ligule.

7. Photo 16 (SCSC-L) shows the TRUE blade/sheath junction + hairs and metric reference. Treat the tiny free membrane as PROVISIONAL / obscured, not photographically measured. To close the 100% gap, gently open SAME true collar under 10–20x with a 1mm ruler, find membranous fringed edge.

8. Compare original archived Matt Lavin source photo 5: awned fertile sessile unit and reduced stalked companion. The photo lacks actual ruler/local voucher, but illustrates true paired structure instead of KR's terminal cluster.

9. Compare KR panels 6 & 7 at equivalent flowering stage: KING RANCH longer multiple terminal racemes from same center; LITTLE more separate SHORT branches from upper leaf axils. Neither stem color nor node hairs alone is conclusive.

10. End with the honest finish test: record cultivar/voucher/locality where available. Do not say microscopic species confirmation FINISHED unless same-voucher attached paired spikelet + free ligule are source photographed to scale.

11. ORIGINAL SOURCE VIEW (NOT INSTALLED): UT Bob Harms DigFlora N. Hays SCSC-disart-w-red.JPG shows an ACTUAL intact A/F/P spikelet complex: A=axis section, F=awned fertile sessile, P=pedicellate rudiment. Compare to our existing Matt Lavin pair macro. Preserve the author's copyright; external research image, not cleared to rehost. Original photograph: https://w3.biosci.utexas.edu/prc/DigFlora/KR/0-BOISS4Web/SCSC-disart-w-red.JPG

12. SOURCE DISSECTION (NOT INSTALLED): Harms SCSC-spkcut.JPG shows separated g1/g2 (glumes), lf/ls (fertile/sterile lemmas) and ps (palea of sterile floret) with physical ruler. These separated organs are NOT shown to be the exact same voucher pair as the linked intact unit. Original photograph: https://w3.biosci.utexas.edu/prc/DigFlora/KR/0-BOISS4Web/SCSC-spkcut.JPG

13. SOURCE LIGULE (NOT INSTALLED): G D Bebeau photographed true split sheath at blade junction, but finger is not mm scale and the actual free fringe is unclear. Collect 1-mm calibrated photo of unfolded membrane tip with outer sheath hairs off to the side.

14. SOURCE HAYS VOUCHER: Hagenbuch and Lemke cite little bluestem Lyday 147 (SWT), Hays Co. This proves a voucher record, not a photo of roots joined to the mature spikelet. Finish with the same plant accession through crown, culm, sheath and mature raceme.

sequence.name: WHOLE ROOTED BUNCH
sequence.photo_role: existing locally archived CC0 bunch image
sequence.evidence: Dense upright perennial shoots and basal tuft clearly visible
sequence.teach: Do not diagnose from winter red color, height or clump form alone; record soil, canopy and shoot arrangement.

sequence.name: FRESH FLOWERS BEFORE SILK
sequence.photo_role: existing Judy Gallagher licensed flower-stage macro
sequence.evidence: Actual anthers emerging alongside one short raceme
sequence.teach: Purple/yellow anthers are the pollen-producing male organs of a bisexual grass flower; fuzzy plumose stigmas may be present. Seed hairs develop later.

sequence.name: WHERE EACH RACEME BEGINS
sequence.photo_role: existing Matt Lavin short silky rachis close-up
sequence.evidence: Individual 2.5–8cm short racemes originate from separate leafy upper culm branches
sequence.teach: Little usually one short raceme per upper branch; KR several longer slender fingers converge near one terminal panicle. Count on SAME whole attached stem.

sequence.name: KEELED SHEATH & EDGE HAIRS
sequence.photo_role: NEW USGS Larry Allain source-labelled leaf-base close-up
sequence.evidence: Real flattened/open sheath and fine overlapping-margin hairs appear; photo does NOT measure membranous ligule
sequence.teach: Carefully separate leaf blade from its sheath; note keeled rib, open margins and the collar. Some sheaths can be hairy; hairy vs smooth is not a safe binary.

sequence.name: TRUE LIGULE (NOT SHEATH HAIRS)
sequence.photo_role: STILL MISSING: actual 10–20x macro with millimeter ruler from live source-confirmed Texas individual
sequence.evidence: FNA reports ligule about 0.5–2 mm; USDA guide allows to 2.5 mm and describes a fringed membrane. Cannot use an image of sheath-margin hairs as the true ligule.
sequence.teach: Photograph the MEMBRANE at the leaf blade/sheath junction, straight on, with 1 mm tick marks and a second side view. Label cilia vs membrane separately.

sequence.name: SESSILE SPIKELET AND STALKED COMPANION
sequence.photo_role: physically archived Matt Lavin public-license source close-up already on card
sequence.evidence: Large awned fertile sessile spikelet and smaller pedicellate companion with hair visible on actual spikelet-bearing axis
sequence.teach: Do not imply every pedicellate companion is minute. In some regional varieties (notably divergens/pinehill), the pedicellate member may be larger, sterile or staminate. Require same-specimen microscope pair and taxon concept.

sequence.name: MATURE AWN, HAIRY RACHIS, DISARTICULATION
sequence.photo_role: existing ripe Matt Lavin plume and archived paired unit
sequence.evidence: Silvery white hairs of maturing axes and awned sessile spikelets visible; exact rachis segmentation and awn insertion unresolved at scale
sequence.teach: White silk is largely rachis internode/pedicel/callus hair. Do not call every silvery fiber a seed hair or claim an awn length without scale.

sequence.name: SIDE-BY-SIDE KR BLUESTEM
sequence.photo_role: two preexisting KR comparator gallery images, one physically archived, from exact taxon
sequence.evidence: Long slender clustered terminal racemes of introduced KR versus multiple separate little short racemes
sequence.teach: If only green leaves/mown plants, use multiple characters; do not authorize invasive removal until confidence is sufficient. KR node pubescence can vary.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — SHORT RACEMES ON SEPARATE UPPER BRANCHES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Native little bluestem: trace ONE flowering stem to multiple short silky racemes, each at the end of a separate upper branch.
field_id_short_tiles.details: The strongest field distinction from introduced KR bluestem is flowering architecture: little bluestem has many short flowering units dispersed among upper leafy branches; KR usually concentrates several longer fingerlike racemes at one terminal region. Inspect the true origin of each unit, not several overlapping grass stems. Color changes seasonally and does not certify identity. Existing source-labelled Texas images show actual short racemes but no connected Hays root-to-floret voucher.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL SOURCE FIELD PANELS — SAME-PLANT VOUCHER STILL NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · PERENNIAL CROWN, KEELED SHEATH AND TRUE LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Tufted or short-rhizomatous perennial; true membranous ligule ~0.5–2 mm (FNA), distinct from long sheath-edge hairs.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Follow flowering culms into the basal crown. FNA allows cespitose OR rhizomatous forms; do not claim all plants have an isolated non-rhizomatous bunch. Sheaths can be rounded or keeled and smooth or hairy. Part an actual leaf sheath at its INNER blade junction: the 0.5–2 mm ligule is a small membranous edge, sometimes fringed; conspicuous hairs outside the collar or along the sheath are NOT the free ligule tip. The Harms SCSC-L and USGS images show real sheath/collar areas, but the unfolded free tip remains unmeasured.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL COLLAR PHOTOS — FREE LIGULE TIP WITH 1-MM SCALE NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · ATTACHED SESSILE / PEDICELLATE SPIKELET PAIR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Sessile fertile spikelets ~3–11 mm; companion pedicellate spikelets ~0.7–10 mm across FNA's variable species concept.
field_id_short_tiles.details: On a single mature hairy raceme, find the sessile spikelet attached directly to the axis and its companion on a short pedicel. FNA gives pedicels ~3–7.5 mm, rachis internodes ~3–7 mm, and pedicellate units that may be sterile OR staminate, with or without a short awn. Do not teach that every companion is a tiny fixed sterile nub. Existing Harms and Matt Lavin closeups document paired structures but do not establish one measured attached pair and a dissection from the same vouchered plant.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL PAIR PHOTO — SAME-UNIT SCALE AND DISSECTION MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES / LEMMA / BENT AWN MEASUREMENTS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Sessile glumes ~5–10 mm in WFO's broad treatment; FNA fertile spikelet ~3–11 mm and upper-lemma awn ~2.5–17 mm.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Each sessile fertile spikelet has TWO glumes enclosing florets; separate first and second glumes before measuring. WFO's historical broad treatment describes glumes ~5–10 mm, while FNA emphasizes the species' variation (sessile spikelets ~3–11 mm). The upper fertile lemma bears a twisted/bent awn ~2.5–17 mm (FNA); reduced lower floret parts can be hidden. The detached Harms SCSC-9 figure shows real anatomical pieces but is not independently linked to the same mature attached unit in SCSC-s. Never infer an awn insertion, lower lemma or glume from gross seedhead pixels.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED RANGES + SOURCE DISSECTION — ONE ATTACHED MEASURED UNIT NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES / KR WARNING
field_id_short_tiles.short: Separate little bluestem from KR bluestem by branch origins and reproductive pairs, not red color or one node-hair rule.
field_id_short_tiles.details: KR bluestem (Bothriochloa ischaemum) usually presents several longer fingerlike racemes near a terminal center; little bluestem has short silky racemes along separate leafy upper branches. Big bluestem (Andropogon gerardii) has a few stout terminal racemes and commonly substantial pedicellate spikelets. Silver bluestem (Bothriochloa laguroides) has whitish flowering branches and can confuse distant views; cane bluestem (Bothriochloa barbinodis) has conspicuously bearded nodes. Node hair on KR can vary by taxonomic treatment, so a 'hairless node = KR' shortcut is unsafe. If immature or only vegetative, retain bluestem sp. pending flowering evidence.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD COMPARISON READY — NO SINGLE-COLOR/HAIR IDENTIFICATION
